shows: A conditional simulation of the 20–24 July 2006 Phoenix heat wave in which the grid is fully nonoperational across the city's municipal extent: 48 hours of complete blackout for every residential structure, then power restored over the remaining 72 hours of the heat wave in order of proximity to substations, with all residents assumed to stay in their homes. Table 1 gives Phoenix's population as 1,445,630. Modelled heat-related deaths over the five days are about 13,250 with power off (the paper's 'approximate total') versus 19 with power on; 13,231 additional deaths is the difference of those two totals. Modelled heat-related ED visits are about 816,570 with power off versus 260 with power on, more than 50% of the population.
limits: A published simulation, not observed mortality or morbidity; the authors note that none of the study cities has experienced a concurrent heat wave and blackout of this intensity and duration. The totals are approximate point estimates with no interval. Residents are held at home and no individual adaptation, evacuation, cooling-centre operation or other emergency response is modelled; the authors also say overwhelmed emergency departments could make mortality higher than they estimate, so the figure is not an upper bound. Exposure passes through a new indoor-outdoor 'analog temperature' conversion into exposure-response functions derived from outdoor temperatures, which adds exposure-model uncertainty. ED visits are predicted heat-related visits, not serious injuries, and far exceed Phoenix's stated fewer than 3,000 ED beds. Transfer depends on a citywide footprint, this outage profile, this weather and near-universal central air conditioning (99% of homes in Table 1). Table 1 attributes the 1,445,630 population to the 2010 Census, while the Results relate the death total to 'the synthetic population'. The 13,231 difference inherits the imprecision of two approximate totals.

locator: Healthcare Facility Preparedness, printed pp. 3-9 (PDF pp. 7-13); Appendix A, Overview of Temporary Power, printed p. 22 (PDF p. 26); Appendix B, Facts, Planning Assumptions, and Critical Considerations, printed pp. 30-31 (PDF pp. 34-35). August 2019 edition.
shows: FEMA's August 2019 guidance on healthcare facilities and power outages records these limits on backup power. Regulations do not mandate emergency standby power for all existing functions; few facilities, especially large ones, have full generator redundancy for their total operating capacity; and air conditioning is often not connected to backup power. Generators require a constant fuel supply, and stored fuel can degrade. Stored-energy (battery) devices used alone are often sized for 90 minutes, enough for safe egress. As a state example, Florida, as a result of Hurricane Irma in 2017, requires skilled nursing and assisted living facilities to have generators powering air conditioning that can hold an ambient temperature of no more than 81 degrees for 96 hours after an outage. The document excerpts two planning considerations from the federal Power Outage Incident Annex: the backup-generator failure rate will rise to approximately 15 percent after 24 hours of continuous use, and dialysis centers generally do not have backup generators, though they may shift patients to other facilities in their network.
limits: Planning guidance, not a measurement of backup endurance in any incident. It gives no national on-site fuel-duration requirement for hospitals and no typical generator run time in hours, so it does not supply the selected 24-hour clinical backup endurance or its 8-96 hour range. The 96-hour figure is one state's post-2017 rule for nursing and assisted living air conditioning; the guidance notes it need not cover whole facilities, and it is neither a hospital requirement nor a demonstrated duration. The 90-minute figure applies to batteries used alone for egress, not to generator-backed systems. The approximately 15 percent failure rate after 24 hours is a planning assumption carried from the federal annex without a stated data source, sample or definition (cumulative versus per-hour), and it is not an observed failure frequency. The dialysis statement is a qualitative generalisation. The guidance is US-specific and dated August 2019 (later code or rule changes were not checked); its case studies are hurricanes (Sandy, Irma), and it does not analyse a cyber-induced grid outage.

shows: For New York City during the 14-15 August 2003 blackout (power lost citywide from 4:11 pm on 14 August), Anderson and Bell estimate about 90 excess all-cause deaths (95% CI 46-138): total mortality rose 28% (95% CI 15-44) over a baseline of 319 deaths expected for the blackout period had the blackout not occurred. Non-accidental mortality rose 25% (12%-41%) and accidental mortality 122% (28%-287%). Neither day was a heatwave day. The authors found no short-term mortality displacement; mortality remained slightly elevated through August 2003. The city health department had counted six deaths directly attributable to the blackout, mostly carbon monoxide poisoning.
limits: One urban blackout, analysed as the two calendar days 14-15 August. The excess is a time-series model estimate (overdispersed Poisson regression adjusted for temperature, dew point, day of week and trends) for the blackout days, not a count of certified deaths and not a per-day hazard. Weather was hot but not extreme for August and neither day was a heatwave day, so the estimate does not transfer directly to an extreme-heat outage such as the Phoenix calibration. The authors suggest New York's high-rise buildings and dependence on public transport may make it particularly vulnerable. The figures are population-wide all-cause mortality; they give no risk for any medical-dependency cohort and cannot be scaled per capita or per outage-hour without an explicit transfer argument. Pollution could not be fully analysed because monitors were interrupted.

shows: Among 45,439 long-stay residents of 1,174 Texas nursing homes, weekly mortality was significantly higher in facilities that reported a power or water outage during Winter Storm Uri than in those that did not. The difference-in-differences estimate is a 0.13% (95% CI 0.03%-0.23%) higher weekly mortality rate, where the rate is the percentage of residents who died in a week. It compares weeks 2-5 after the storm with weeks 4 to 1 before it, and the abstract places the higher mortality in weeks 3-5. Post- versus pre-storm mortality changes were -0.15% in outage facilities and -0.28% in the others. In sensitivity analyses, facilities reporting both power and water loss had a difference of 0.60% (0.04%-1.16%), while the power-only difference was not statistically significant. Facilities did not report how long outages lasted.
limits: The main exposure is loss of power or water, pooled. The power-only contrast was not statistically significant, so the 0.13 estimate is not an electricity-outage effect by itself. Outages were self-reported voluntarily to the state with no duration, so no per-day or dose-response hazard can be derived. The authors note possible misclassification, which they say may understate the effect, and did not measure concurrent COVID-19 or influenza. The effect is a pooled weekly-rate difference over four post-storm weeks, arising from a smaller post-storm mortality decline in outage facilities. It concerns care-dependent long-stay residents in severe cold, with a lag of weeks, and does not transfer to home equipment users, inpatients or a heat outage without the same exposure definition and weekly risk accounting.

The unit is the ED visit, not the patient: the sample has no patient identifier, so repeat visits cannot be removed. The 3.5% is case fatality among visits that reached an ED; the authors attribute its lowness partly to the most severe cases dying at the scene, so it excludes pre-hospital deaths and is neither a population heat-stroke fatality nor a fatality for untreated or delayed cases. shows: An observational series of 58 patients with classic heat stroke admitted to Chicago-area intensive care units during the 12-20 July 1995 heat wave; classic heat-stroke patients not admitted to intensive care were excluded. quotes.text: Setting: Intensive care units in the Chicago area. Patients: 58 patients admitted to the hospital from 12 July to 20 July 1995 who met the case definition of classic heat stroke.

In-hospital mortality was 21%. Most survivors recovered near-normal renal, hematologic, and respiratory status, but disability persisted, resulting in moderate to severe functional impairment in 33% of patients at hospital discharge.
At 1 year, no patient had improved functional status, and an additional 28% of patients had died.
Patients who met the case definition of classic heat stroke but were not admitted to the intensive care unit were excluded from further analysis.
Twelve patients died (20.7%).
At discharge, 11 patients did not have neurologic impairment (24%), 20 had minimal impairment (43%), and 15 had moderate to severe impairment (33%).
One-year follow-up was attempted in all 46 survivors. Fourteen patients could not be located. Five patients were verified as alive but could not be contacted.
The 1-year mortality rate was 28% (9 of 32 patients); this percentage includes patients who were verified as alive but were not contacted.

shows: The National Hurricane Center's report on Hurricane Beryl (version of 1 May 2025, amending the report of 23 January 2025) records that Beryl made its Texas landfall near Matagorda at 0840 UTC on 8 July 2024 and passed over the western side of the Houston metropolitan area. The report counts 34 deaths indirectly caused by the storm in the United States, all in Texas; fourteen of them were due to heat-induced hyperthermia caused by widespread electrical outages. Among the other indirect deaths, one followed a fall in a home after an electrical outage, one occurred when an electrical outage caused a breathing machine to fail, and two were due to carbon monoxide poisoning; the causes of the rest were not available as of writing. These indirect deaths are counted separately from the deaths the storm directly caused. Citing media reports, the report states that almost 3 million people lost power due to the cyclone, 2.7 million of them in southeastern Texas.
limits: The outage figure is a media-reported count of people relayed by the report, not a utility customer-account count, and the report gives no outage durations or restoration timeline. The fourteen hyperthermia deaths are a tally of reported indirect deaths as of the report's writing; the report does not describe how deaths were ascertained or attributed and gives no excess-mortality estimate, so it is not a complete count of outage-related heat mortality. The report states no post-storm air temperature, heat index or indoor conditions, so it provides no basis for comparing heat exposure with a Phoenix extreme-heat scenario. It gives no ages, medical dependency, places of death or response measures (such as cooling centres) for the decedents. A hurricane combines wind, flood and debris-clearing hazards with the outage, so these counts do not isolate an outage-only effect, and a single event supports no rate.

locator: Community Impact, 'Beryl shines spotlight on lack of backup generators at city-run facilities', published 10 July 2024: 'Catch up quick' paragraphs 1-3 and 'Also of note' paragraph 1
shows: Community Impact reported on 10 July 2024, from a Houston City Council meeting that morning, that many multiservice centres pre-designated as potential cooling areas before Hurricane Beryl 'could not be used because they did not have power', according to the city's acting director of public safety and homeland security. He said the city averages about 58 cooling centres per day during dangerous heat when there are no electricity problems, but that because of power issues after Beryl it 'had only been able to operate 27', with five more opened on 10 July with the YMCA. At one multiservice centre a backup generator was in place but the centre still lost power, and the mayor had complained on 9 July of missing backup generators at city facilities including multiservice centres.
limits: A news report of officials' remarks, not an audited count. The 58 is an average number of centres the city operates per day in ordinary heat periods, not a fixed inventory of designated sites, so 27 of 58 is a ratio of daily operations, not a share of designated sites that were usable. The 27 has no stated time within 10 July, and neither count gives capacity in people, opening hours or attendance. The article does not say when the first centre opened after landfall or how the count grew; it attributes the shortfall to lack of power and does not separate storm damage from outage effects. A forecast hurricane with storm damage differs from a no-notice cyber blackout, so applying these counts to one is a modelling judgement. A council member said the city should have its own comprehensive plan, separate from the fire department's, for setting up cooling centres after a disaster; the figures reflect one city's preparedness at that time.

shows: A survey-calibrated computable general equilibrium study of Commonwealth Edison's service area (3.8 million customers in the greater Chicago area and beyond) measures losses as deviations from the baseline over the three-month period that begins with the interruption. The abstract states that 1-, 3- and 14-day interruptions reduce the service area's three-month GDP by USD 1.8 bn (1.3%), 3.7 bn (2.6%) and 15.2 bn (10.4%), with 71-88% of losses from disequilibrium responses to shortages. The results text gives USD 0.3, 0.8 and 4.9 bn from market-equilibrium effects of the curtailment alone, USD 2.2, 4.3 and 17.1 bn once survey-derived disequilibrium adjustments are added, and USD 1.9, 3.7 and 15.2 bn with doubled backup generation; the disequilibrium effects bring losses to about 1%, 3% and 9-11% of baseline GDP.
limits: The abstract's dollar figures equal the doubled-backup-generation results, not the base case; its percentages and its 71-88% disequilibrium share fit the base case (derived: the base-case losses and the abstract percentages imply one quarterly baseline of about USD 164-165 bn, which the doubled-backup losses do not). Ratios of the percentage loss to a proportional shutdown of the area for the outage days (percentage divided by outage days / 91.25) are about 1.2, 0.8 and 0.7 for 1, 3 and 14 days; they are derived, not reported, and are not a share of output permanently lost, because they combine curtailed production, resilience-tactic costs and economy-wide spillovers within one quarter. Behaviour comes from a survey about hypothetical outages, the authors caution that results need further research before generalising to other regions and contexts, survey responses are pooled across seasons, and the published text does not state a price year.

The report was written within about 96 hours of ESET sharing malware hashes with Dragos on 8 June 2017 (pp. 3 and 5), by a vendor whose customers had received a separate intelligence report. Parts of the toolkit were unavailable to Dragos at publication: it confirmed that the IEC 101, IEC 61850 and OPC DA modules exist but did not have them. On the SIPROTEC denial-of-service module, the report says Dragos could not validate that it exists (p. 22) and that Dragos has independent but unconfirmed evidence of it (p. 25). shows: In this peer-reviewed simulation study of a concurrent heat wave and citywide blackout in Atlanta, Detroit and Phoenix, the authors state that none of the three cities had developed an emergency response plan for a compound heat-wave and widespread-outage event. Each city had designated public cooling centres for extreme heat: 18 in Phoenix, 12 in Detroit and 5 in Atlanta. The authors judge that 'the size and number of such facilities' would accommodate no more than 1-2% of the urban population during a concurrent heat wave and blackout. None of the cities' cooling-centre plans required back-up power generating capacity to keep mechanical cooling running under blackout conditions. The authors conclude that such an event would require a far more extensive network of emergency cooling centres, with mandated back-up power generation. The statement cites city and county cooling-centre web pages (references 37-41); the Phoenix-area source is Maricopa County's 'Cooling Stations and Water Donation Sites' page (2020).
limits: The 1-2% share is the authors' judgement, stated jointly for three cities. The article gives no per-site capacity, no summed capacity, no population arithmetic and no method for turning 'size and number' into a share, so it is not a facility-capacity audit and a Phoenix-only share cannot be read from it. The 18 is a count of designated sites on public web listings in 2020, not a count of places, beds or staffed hours, and it describes an ordinary-heat network rather than a blackout operation. The back-up-power finding concerns what the cooling-centre plans require; it does not establish that individual sites lack generators. The statement is silent on hotels, private homes that keep power, workplaces and other cooled space, and on uptake, transport and activation time. It is a 2020 planning snapshot, not a description of current plans. This statement is the authors' planning review within the paper; the building-energy simulation itself does not model cooling-centre use.

locator: Caton et al., Disaster Med Public Health Prep 2025;19:e158, Brief Report, Cambridge Core open-access full-text HTML (no printed pagination): Abstract (Results); 'Methods' paragraphs 1 and 3; 'Results' paragraph 2; 'Discussion' paragraph 1
shows: Houston Health Department analysts compared daily emergency department (ED) visit counts from their syndromic surveillance system, with patient and facility in Harris, Fort Bend or Montgomery County, for Day 0 to Day 14 after Hurricane Beryl reached Houston on 8 July 2024. The baseline was the 14 days before the storm, and the comparison used t tests. Visits were significantly higher than expected (P<0.05) for total visits and acute cardiac events (acute myocardial infarction or cardiac arrest) on Days 1-2 and for heat-related illness on Days 1-3. They were also higher for carbon monoxide poisoning on Days 1-9, for dialysis on Days 0-3 and Day 7, and for medication refills on Days 0-14 except Day 10. Stroke visits stayed within the expected range. The authors say the increases were most marked on the days that coincided with mass power outages (Days 0 through 3).
limits: The text reports statistical significance only. It gives no visit counts, rates, excess numbers or effect sizes; daily volumes appear only as three-day moving averages in a figure. It therefore supplies no rate per person exposed to the outage, and it has no mortality or admission outcome. Single-day t tests across six conditions and total visits over fifteen days have no stated correction for multiple comparisons. The abstract and the Results disagree on the windows. The abstract gives medication refills as Day 1-9 and dialysis as Day 0-3, while the Results give refills on Days 0-14 except Day 10 and add dialysis on Day 7. Categories come from chief-complaint and discharge-diagnosis fields. The hurricane itself, including wind damage and debris removal, is a co-exposure that the design does not separate from the outage; the attribution to outages rests on timing. Temperatures were below Houston heat-advisory criteria and far below a 32-45 C Phoenix heat wave. A forecast hurricane in Houston also differs from a no-notice cyber outage. The study supports outage-period demand beyond heat illness (dialysis, medication refills, carbon monoxide, cardiac events) as a mechanism, not a magnitude for another city, climate or outage cause.

shows: A New York City health department time-series study (Poisson regression with distributed lags, adjusted for heat index or temperature, day of week, holiday, year and within-season trend) compared deaths among city residents on outage days with non-outage days in May-September study periods. Exposure to the 14-15 August 2003 blackout, which affected all 66 NYC electric-grid networks and about 3 million electricity customers (8 million residents), was defined as a death occurring on 14-15 August 2003. Lags were examined only as the same day plus the 1, 2 or 3 previous days (lag01, lag02, lag03). All-cause mortality was positively associated with all three individual outages (1999 Washington Heights, 2003 citywide, 2006 Long Island City), but only the 2003 association was statistically significant. For all-cause mortality the associations 'were similar at all multiday lags, with a slight peak at lag01' for 2003 (cumulative relative risk 1.41, 95% CI 1.24-1.60) and for 2006 (1.42, 0.92-2.18), and peaked at lag03 for 1999 (2.40, 0.69-8.36). External-cause mortality in 2003 had a larger lag01 estimate (2.39, 1.46-3.93). The authors describe the 2003 mortality associations as 'immediate'.
limits: The analysis window ends three days after an outage day, so the study cannot show whether excess deaths continued after day 3; it neither establishes nor rules out a longer tail. Similar cumulative estimates from lag01 to lag03 suggest little added excess on lag days 2 and 3 within that window, but that is a reading of the reported pattern, not a separate test. The exposure is a calendar outage day for the whole resident population, not the onset of unmet need in a device-dependent or home-care cohort, so these lags are not the time from fatal illness onset to death and cannot set a death-lag distribution directly. A cumulative relative risk for the whole city population is not a per-person hazard per unmet day and does not say who died. The 2003 exposure covers two calendar days; Table 1 lists no weather event for it (maximum heat index 94 F), and the discussion attributes some harm to loss of transit and people walking home, so longer, hotter or deliberately caused outages may differ. Exposure was assigned by residential address, so the study could not confirm that decedents were at home or lacked alternative power. Individual lag-day estimates are in supplemental Table S1, which was not retrieved. The 2003 analysis uses the same event and overlapping death records as an earlier study of this blackout, so the two are not independent replications.

shows: In a second analysis the authors pooled localized outages across NYC electric-grid networks in 2002-2014, using New York State Public Service Commission outage reports. A network-day counted as an outage if at least 1,000 customers (May-September) or at least 75 customers (October-April) were without power at any point, and every residence in that network was then treated as exposed although generally only a fraction lost power; outage duration could not be ascertained. Pooled warm-weather outages were not associated with all-cause or nonexternal mortality but were associated with renal-disease hospitalizations at later lags, most strongly at lag 2 (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.03-1.33). limits: Exposure is assigned to whole networks in which only a small share of customers usually lost power (mostly under 15% of network customers in Table 2, apart from the July 2010 heat-wave outages), without duration, so the null warm-weather mortality result cannot be read as evidence that small or short outages are harmless, and the positive estimates are diluted by an unknown amount. Different customer thresholds in the two seasons limit seasonal comparison. The events are mostly weather-related or unexplained distribution outages in a dense city with underground networks, not a deliberate regional loss of transmission control. The lags again stop at three days. Relative risks for all residents do not identify device-dependent or home-care cohorts and give no per-day hazard.

shows: A CDC retrospective analysis of 2012 Truven MarketScan employer-sponsored insurance claims counted enrollees who lived at home and depended on electrically powered durable medical equipment to sustain life. Cases were enrollees with 2012 outpatient claims for ventilators or oxygen concentrators who also had claims for health care delivered in the patient's home. After weighting, 366,619 (95% CI 365,700-367,537) of about 175 million employer-sponsored privately insured people met the definition, a prevalence of 218.2 per 100,000 covered lives (95% CI 217.7-218.8). Applying that prevalence to the 2012 US Census population estimate gave an all-payer approximation of 685,482 (95% CI 683,810-687,153) electricity-dependent people living at home. The authors say this national total may underestimate the true population and should be considered only an approximation.
limits: Prevalence is measured only among the employer-sponsored privately insured, including Medicare-eligible people with employer-sponsored supplemental cover. The all-payer count assumes that this prevalence holds for the uninsured, Medicaid and Medicare-only populations, which the authors say may bias it. Its confidence interval reflects sampling in the claims data only, not that extrapolation. The definition covers only ventilators and oxygen concentrators with home-care claims. It excludes CPAP and BiPAP, powered wheelchairs, home dialysis, feeding and infusion pumps, and anyone whose equipment generated no 2012 claim, so it is narrower than definitions that count all powered medical equipment. "To sustain life" is the authors' framing of these device classes; the study does not measure clinical dependence or time to harm. The counts are for 2012, with no later growth measured. The study gives no count for any particular 20-million-person region: a per-capita transfer (218.2 per 100,000 x 20,000,000 = about 43,600) is user arithmetic, not a study result.

shows: The authors state that durable medical equipment can run on batteries for a limited time for transport and mobility, and that oxygen-concentrator battery life can be around 2 to 4 hours, extendable to up to 12 hours with backup external packs at the lowest settings. In the discussion they describe the concentrator as a device that lets people move about and even travel without a canister or tank, and that is limited by its battery life when unplugged. At the lowest settings most last 3 to 4 hours (selected models up to 6 hours), and a few models 8 or more hours with an additional battery. Planners cannot assume patients use the minimal setting: higher settings shorten battery life significantly, and patients on higher settings are more likely to decompensate faster and need medical intervention sooner.
limits: These are background statements in the introduction and discussion, not results of the claims analysis. No source is cited for the hour figures, and the models, flow settings and test conditions are not identified. The two passages give different ranges: 2 to 4 hours, extendable to 12, versus 3 to 4 hours, up to 6, and 8 or more with an additional battery. The article does not say how many of the counted concentrator users have a battery-capable portable unit rather than a mains-only stationary one, a spare battery or backup cylinders. It therefore gives no distribution of home backup endurance and cannot support a single cohort-wide value. locator: Materials and Methods, Health Impact Assessment, Steps 3-7.
shows: The study fits a mixed-effect linear regression of IET on outdoor airport temperature with building and personal characteristics, and rearranges it to give an "analog" outdoor temperature T' for each person's daily IET. It sums each person's heat-attributable burdens over the five-day heat wave, and limits each person's aggregate risk to a maximum of 1.
